title: No Notes 2026
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer argues that teachers should stop asking students to copy notes from the board during lessons. Drawing on the many lessons he observes, he lists four problems: students learn almost nothing while copying, the practice eats finite lesson time, it gives a false sense of achievement, and it breaks the smooth, synchronised flow of a lesson. He then works through the common objections, including revision, Ofsted, evidence of learning and preparing students for university, and answers each in turn. His alternative is to provide any notes students truly need and spend the saved minutes checking understanding with questions and independent practice. The piece is a concrete, practice-level argument that connects cognitive claims about attention and memory to everyday classroom routines. Boxer admits he is not normally a ban-minded writer but makes an exception here.
points: Boxer's informal test, asking a student mid-copy to recall what they just wrote, finds they cannot report more than the last word or two, which suggests copying is cognitively close to empty.
Copying takes real time at roughly 13-15 words per minute for secondary students, and fast copiers fall out of step with the lesson, which damages its smoothness.
Copied notes create a false sense of security that later shows up as ineffective copious-note revision before exams.
The objections about revision, Ofsted and university note-taking do not require in-class copying; supplying notes and using the time for retrieval questions meets each concern.
After an explanation the first move should be a check for understanding through questions, not a copying task.
quotes: To date, no student has ever been able to tell me more than the last word or two they wrote. Certainly not anything approaching a sentence or full definition.
Lesson time is finite, and any time students spend doing one thing is time spent not doing something else.

Students think that by writing things down in their book they have achieved something in the lesson. Aside from the complacency this can lead to in the short term, often the same students will then “revise” for their exams by writing copious notes, an activity unlikely to be effective in terms of learning.
Rather than create classrooms within classrooms, teachers should aim to build a sense of collective intellectual endeavour and routine.

If there are notes we want students to use to revise from, we should just provide them with those notes, save the copying time and spend it more profitably on intellectual work like mini-whiteboard questions or independent practice.
The first response is that copied notes are, of course, not evidence of learning at all: they are evidence of copying.
Instead, students should spend lesson time actively thinking: answering questions or processing and generating information.
Copying from the board is a rare thing in education: something that most teachers could completely eliminate from their practice and see no downside at all.
